lessonTitle: Hypertension: Causes, Target-Organ Damage and Drug Mechanisms

blocks.text: A 48-year-old man goes to an optician for new glasses. Through the ophthalmoscope the optometrist sees flame-shaped retinal haemorrhages and swollen optic discs, and measures a blood pressure of 190/115 mmHg. He feels perfectly well. Hypertension is the great silent disease: it damages the eye, brain, heart and kidney for years before any symptom appears.

blocks.markdown: Arterial blood pressure (BP) is the lateral pressure that circulating blood exerts on artery walls, written as systolic over diastolic in mmHg. **Hypertension** is a sustained elevation of BP. Exact thresholds vary between guidelines and between clinic and home readings, but a persistently elevated clinic reading of about 140/90 mmHg or higher is the traditional cut-off. Because BP is a continuous risk factor, cardiovascular risk rises smoothly with BP rather than switching on at a threshold.

blocks.title: Mean arterial pressure
blocks.text: Mean arterial pressure (MAP) is the time-averaged pressure driving blood through the organs. Because the heart spends about two thirds of each cycle in diastole, MAP is estimated as diastolic pressure plus one third of the pulse pressure, where pulse pressure is systolic minus diastolic.

blocks.caption: MAP estimate (mmHg). SBP = systolic, DBP = diastolic pressure.
Pressure = flow x resistance. CO = cardiac output (L/min); SVR = systemic vascular resistance (mmHg per L/min). Central venous pressure is neglected as it is small.
Poiseuille relationship for a rigid tube: resistance R rises steeply as vessel radius r falls, so small arteriolar narrowing raises SVR substantially.

blocks.title: Estimating MAP and the haemodynamic driver
blocks.prompt: A patient has BP 150/96 mmHg and a cardiac output of 5.0 L/min. Estimate MAP and SVR.

steps.text: Rearrange MAP = CO x SVR: SVR = MAP / CO = 114 / 5.0 = 22.8 mmHg per L/min.
Interpretation: with a normal cardiac output, the raised pressure is explained by raised resistance, which is the typical pattern of established primary hypertension.

blocks.answer: MAP is about 114 mmHg and SVR about 22.8 mmHg per L/min, so the hypertension is resistance-driven.

blocks.markdown:
### Primary versus secondary hypertension

In about 90-95% of adults no single cause is found; this is **primary (essential) hypertension**. It is polygenic and multifactorial: ageing stiffens large arteries, and obesity, high salt intake, alcohol, inactivity and family history all contribute, producing an increase in peripheral resistance and impaired renal sodium excretion. It usually presents after the age of 40 and is often mild to moderate.

**Secondary hypertension** has an identifiable, sometimes curable cause. It is suspected when hypertension starts young (under about 30) or suddenly, is severe or resistant to several drugs, or comes with clues such as low potassium, an abdominal bruit, or episodic symptoms.

rows: Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome)
Autonomous aldosterone raises sodium retention and volume; suppresses renin
Low serum potassium, high aldosterone with low renin
Renal artery stenosis
Reduced renal perfusion activates renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS)
Abdominal bruit; atherosclerosis in older patients, fibromuscular dysplasia in young women
Chronic kidney disease / renal parenchymal disease
Sodium and water retention plus RAAS activation
Raised creatinine, proteinuria; the commonest secondary cause
Phaeochromocytoma
Catecholamine-secreting adrenal medullary tumour
Episodic headache, sweating, palpitations; paroxysmal BP surges
Coarctation of the aorta
Narrowing of the aortic isthmus raises upper-body pressure
Radio-femoral delay; lower BP in legs than arms
Cushing syndrome
Cortisol excess with mineralocorticoid effect, sodium retention
Central obesity, striae, bruising

blocks.title: Recognising a secondary cause
blocks.prompt: A 27-year-old woman has BP 165/100 mmHg on repeated measurement. Serum potassium is 2.9 mmol/L (laboratory reference about 3.5-5.0). Plasma renin is suppressed and aldosterone is raised. What is the most likely diagnosis and why?

steps.text: Age under 30 with sustained hypertension already points towards a secondary cause rather than essential hypertension.
Hypokalaemia in an untreated hypertensive patient suggests excess mineralocorticoid action: aldosterone drives sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion in the collecting duct.

High aldosterone with suppressed renin means aldosterone is not being driven by the renin-angiotensin system; the volume expansion it causes switches renin off. This is autonomous aldosterone production.
In renal artery stenosis, renin would be high, not suppressed, so that diagnosis is less likely.

blocks.answer: Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome), for example from an adrenal adenoma.

blocks.markdown:
### Target-organ damage

Persistently raised pressure damages the circulation and the organs it feeds. In small vessels it causes **hyaline arteriolosclerosis**: leaked plasma proteins thicken arteriolar walls, narrowing the lumen. In the kidney this produces **nephrosclerosis**, with proteinuria and slow loss of glomerular filtration rate. In very severe, rapidly rising pressure (accelerated or malignant hypertension) **hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis** appears, with concentric 'onion-skin' thickening and fibrinoid necrosis, which can cause acute kidney injury, papilloedema and encephalopathy.

The heart faces a chronically raised afterload. The left ventricle compensates by **concentric left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH)**: cardiomyocytes thicken, the wall stiffens, and oxygen demand rises, which predisposes to ischaemia, diastolic dysfunction, heart failure and atrial fibrillation. Large arteries develop accelerated atherosclerosis and aortic dissection risk.

items: Brain: stroke (ischaemic from atherosclerosis, haemorrhagic from rupture of small penetrating arteries), small-vessel disease and vascular dementia, hypertensive encephalopathy.
Heart: LVH, coronary artery disease, heart failure, atrial fibrillation.
Kidney: nephrosclerosis leading to chronic kidney disease.
Eye: hypertensive retinopathy, with arteriolar narrowing, haemorrhages, exudates and, in malignant hypertension, papilloedema.
Aorta and peripheral arteries: aneurysm, dissection, peripheral arterial disease.

rows: ACE inhibitor (for example ramipril)
Blocks conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, lowering vasoconstriction and aldosterone; also reduces bradykinin breakdown
Dry cough (bradykinin), first-dose hypotension, hyperkalaemia, angioedema
Angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB, for example losartan)
Blocks the AT1 receptor so angiotensin II cannot act
Hyperkalaemia; cough is uncommon because bradykinin is unaffected
Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (for example amlodipine)
Blocks L-type calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle, causing arteriolar vasodilatation
Ankle oedema, flushing, headache
Thiazide-like diuretic (for example indapamide)
Inhibits the Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule, causing natriuresis and early volume loss, then reduced vascular resistance
Hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia, hyperuricaemia
blocks.caption: First-line antihypertensive classes (drug names are teaching examples, not advice)

blocks.title: Why the drug classes work
blocks.text: Every antihypertensive acts on one term of BP = CO x SVR. Diuretics reduce volume and so cardiac output initially; vasodilators (calcium channel blockers) and RAAS blockers lower vascular resistance. Choice depends on age, ethnic background, comorbidity and tolerability, and the details vary between guidelines.

blocks.title: Do not stop at the number
blocks.text: A single high clinic reading is not a diagnosis. Confirm with repeated measurements or ambulatory or home monitoring, because white-coat effects are common. Severe hypertension with signs of acute organ damage is an emergency and needs urgent specialist care.

points: Primary hypertension is multifactorial and accounts for most cases; secondary hypertension has an identifiable cause and is suspected when onset is young, sudden, severe or resistant.

Sustained hypertension causes hyaline arteriolosclerosis, nephrosclerosis, LVH, stroke, retinopathy and accelerated atherosclerosis; malignant hypertension adds fibrinoid necrosis and onion-skin change.
Antihypertensives act on the RAAS (ACE inhibitors, ARBs), vascular smooth muscle calcium channels (dihydropyridine CCBs) or distal tubular sodium reabsorption (thiazide-like diuretics).

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman has several months of episodic pounding headaches, sweating and palpitations. During an attack her BP is 210/120 mmHg, and between attacks it is lower. Which secondary cause is most likely?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: paroxysmal catecholamine release from an adrenal medullary tumour produces the classic triad of headache, sweating and palpitations with BP surges.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: Conn syndrome gives sustained hypertension with hypokalaemia, not paroxysmal adrenergic symptoms.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: coarctation causes a fixed BP difference between arms and legs and radio-femoral delay, not episodic attacks.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: essential hypertension is sustained and does not produce paroxysmal adrenergic symptoms.

questions.explanation: A catecholamine-secreting tumour of the adrenal medulla releases adrenaline and noradrenaline in bursts, causing episodic vasoconstriction and tachycardia. The paroxysmal pattern with headache, sweating and palpitations is the key discriminator from sustained causes of secondary hypertension.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man has had poorly controlled hypertension for 20 years. Renal biopsy shows thickened, glassy pink walls of the small afferent arterioles with narrowed lumens. Which term describes this change?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: leaked plasma proteins and basement membrane thickening give homogeneous pink arteriolar walls in long-standing hypertension.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis shows concentric onion-skin layering and occurs in malignant (accelerated) hypertension.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: fibrinoid necrosis is a feature of malignant hypertension, not of chronic benign change.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: amyloid is a different protein deposition disease and is not the expected finding here.

questions.explanation: Chronic moderate hypertension damages arteriolar endothelium so plasma proteins leak into and thicken the wall, producing hyaline arteriolosclerosis. This causes nephrosclerosis and gradual loss of renal function.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man starts an ACE inhibitor and two weeks later develops a persistent dry cough. What is the most likely mechanism?

options.text: Accumulation of bradykinin because its breakdown is reduced
Excess angiotensin II acting on AT1 receptors
Direct blockade of calcium channels in bronchial smooth muscle

questions.correctOptionText: Accumulation of bradykinin because its breakdown is reduced

distractorRationale.a: Correct: ACE also degrades bradykinin, which accumulates and irritates airway sensory nerves.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: ACE inhibitors lower, not raise, angiotensin II.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: ACE inhibitors promote natriuresis and do not cause fluid retention.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: calcium channel blockade is not the mechanism of ACE inhibitors and does not explain cough.

questions.explanation: Angiotensin-converting enzyme is the same enzyme that degrades bradykinin, so blocking it raises bradykinin levels and produces a dry cough in a minority of patients. An ARB does not inhibit ACE, which is why it is often substituted.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman is prescribed a thiazide-like diuretic. At which site does this drug class act to cause natriuresis?

options.text: The Na-Cl cotransporter of the distal convoluted tubule
The Na-K-2Cl cotransporter of the thick ascending limb
The aldosterone receptor of the collecting duct
The carbonic anhydrase enzyme of the proximal tubule

questions.correctOptionText: The Na-Cl cotransporter of the distal convoluted tubule

distractorRationale.a: Correct: thiazides block the Na-Cl cotransporter, reducing sodium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this is the target of loop diuretics.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this is the target of aldosterone antagonists such as spironolactone.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: this is the target of acetazolamide.

questions.explanation: Thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics inhibit the Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule. Loop diuretics, mineralocorticoid antagonists and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors act at other nephron sites and are not first-line antihypertensives in the same way.

questions.stem: True or false: left ventricular hypertrophy in chronic hypertension is a compensatory response to pressure overload, but the thickened, stiffer wall increases oxygen demand and the risk of ischaemia and heart failure.
questions.explanation: Raised afterload makes the ventricle thicken concentrically to normalise wall stress. The hypertrophied myocardium stiffens, needs more oxygen and can outgrow its blood supply, which leads to diastolic dysfunction, ischaemia and eventually heart failure.

questions.stem: A patient has a cardiac output of 4.5 L/min and an estimated mean arterial pressure of 135 mmHg. Using MAP = CO x SVR and neglecting central venous pressure, calculate the systemic vascular resistance in mmHg per L/min.
questions.explanation: Rearranging MAP = CO x SVR gives SVR = MAP / CO = 135 / 4.5 = 30 mmHg per L/min. This is well above the normal range, showing that raised resistance rather than raised output is sustaining the high pressure.

questions.stem: In hypertension, arteriolar remodelling narrows the lumen. Treating the arteriole as a rigid tube in which resistance is proportional to 1/r^4, by what factor does resistance increase if the radius falls by 10% (to 0.90 of its original value)? Give a dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: Resistance scales as 1/r^4, so the new resistance is 1/(0.9^4) = 1/0.6561, which is about 1.52 times the original. A small reduction in radius produces a large rise in resistance, which is why modest arteriolar narrowing sustains hypertension.

questions.stem: Distinguish primary from secondary hypertension. Name three secondary causes and state one clinical or laboratory clue for each.
markingGuide: Primary (essential): no single identifiable cause, multifactorial (age, obesity, salt, genetics), about 90-95% of cases, usually later onset
Secondary: identifiable and sometimes curable cause; suspect if young onset, severe, sudden or resistant
Three valid causes with a clue each, for example Conn syndrome with low potassium and high aldosterone to renin ratio
Renal artery stenosis with abdominal bruit, or chronic kidney disease with raised creatinine and proteinuria
Phaeochromocytoma with episodic headache, sweating and palpitations, or coarctation with radio-femoral delay
questions.explanation: Primary hypertension has no single cause and arises from interacting genetic and environmental factors, whereas secondary hypertension results from a specific disease. Identifying the secondary types matters because treating the underlying cause may cure or greatly improve the hypertension.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has had untreated hypertension for 15 years. Describe the target-organ damage you would expect in the heart, brain, kidney and eye, with the underlying mechanism of each.
markingGuide: Heart: pressure overload causes concentric LVH, diastolic dysfunction, ischaemia, heart failure, atrial fibrillation
Brain: stroke (ischaemic and haemorrhagic), small-vessel disease and vascular dementia
Kidney: hyaline arteriolosclerosis causing nephrosclerosis with proteinuria and falling GFR
Eye: hypertensive retinopathy with arteriolar narrowing, haemorrhages, exudates, papilloedema in malignant hypertension
Mechanism linking them: chronic pressure injures endothelium, thickens arteriolar walls and accelerates atherosclerosis
Mention of malignant hypertension features such as fibrinoid necrosis and onion-skin hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis
questions.explanation: Sustained pressure damages arteriolar endothelium and accelerates atherosclerosis, so every organ with a high-flow microcirculation is affected. The heart responds to afterload with hypertrophy, while the brain, kidney and retina show vascular occlusion, rupture or thickening of small arteries.

questions.stem: Match an ACE inhibitor, an angiotensin receptor blocker, a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker and a thiazide-like diuretic to their mechanism of lowering BP. Explain why cough occurs with ACE inhibitors but not ARBs.
markingGuide: ACE inhibitor: blocks conversion of angiotensin I to II, reducing vasoconstriction and aldosterone
ARB: blocks AT1 receptor so angiotensin II cannot act
Dihydropyridine CCB: blocks L-type calcium channels in arteriolar smooth muscle causing vasodilatation
Thiazide-like diuretic: inhibits Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule causing natriuresis and volume reduction
ACE also degrades bradykinin; ACE inhibition raises bradykinin causing cough
ARBs do not inhibit ACE so bradykinin is not increased
questions.explanation: Each drug class intervenes at a different point in the determinants of BP, either on the renin-angiotensin axis, vascular smooth muscle calcium entry or renal sodium handling. Cough is a bradykinin effect of ACE inhibition only, which explains why an ARB is a common alternative.
